content: Conducting situation analyses of palliative care needs is essential for designing and implementing effective palliative care strategies tailored to specific locations and types of humanitarian emergencies or crises. Data on the types of suffering, their prevalence, and the populations most at risk in each type of humanitarian emergency are invaluable for this purpose. Research on the outcomes, effectiveness, value, and quality of palliative care interventions can significantly enhance care delivery. Not all research questions need to be addressed during high-crisis situations, as the vulnerabilities and desperation of affected communities may render such research unethical or undesirable. Some questions, such as those related to vaccine or treatment safety in Phase I clinical trials, can be explored during periods of relative calm. However, certain questions, such as the efficacy of interventions for crush injuries or treatments for rare viral outbreaks like Ebola, can only be answered in the context of an extreme crisis. Therefore, it is crucial to carefully select the environment, population, and intervention for research. Researchers must avoid exploiting the vulnerabilities of crisis-affected populations by pursuing trivial or irrelevant research objectives. At the same time, access to patients in humanitarian settings, including those requiring palliative care, should not be excessively restricted. With appropriate ethical review, it is possible to involve patients in crisis settings, including those nearing the end of life, in research in a manner that respects their dignity and rights. When designing research in humanitarian settings involving individuals with palliative care needs, researchers should adhere to widely accepted ethical standards, such as the Declaration of Helsinki. Local research ethics committee approval should be obtained in advance, as required by the local government. Researchers must respect local cultural norms, obtain meaningful informed consent in a culturally sensitive and non-coercive manner, and be mindful of potential biases introduced by the characteristics of those who agree or decline to participate in palliative care research. The potential benefits of the research must outweigh any potential harms, and patients should not be overburdened with research interventions. However, it is important to recognize that some patients with palliative care needs may wish to contribute to research and find meaning in their participation. Participants must be allowed to decline or withdraw from the research at any time without penalty. Research activities should not impede overall response efforts or the care of research subjects. Material Transfer Agreements should be in place to safeguard the stewardship of personal data or biosamples collected from patients who may not be available for follow-up permissions due to imminent death. In the context of monitored emergency use of unregistered experimental interventions (MEURI), the World Health Organization (WHO) has stated that offering experimental interventions to individual patients on an emergency basis outside clinical trials can be ethically appropriate during outbreaks with high mortality. This must be done with local approval and oversight, adequate voluntary and informed consent, and assurance that the intervention is monitored and data is formally collected to support future research. By definition, MEURI primarily involves patients with life-threatening illnesses for whom palliative and supportive care are the only alternatives.
